reading.title: Two Latin Roots That Sort Harm from Help
reading.purpose: Explore how the Latin roots bene and mal appear across medicine, engineering, and daily life.
paras: Two short Latin roots—bene, meaning good, and mal, meaning bad—quietly shape dozens of English words across science, law, and everyday speech. Knowing this pair helps you decode unfamiliar terms on sight. In nutrition and medicine, a beneficial habit, such as daily walking or getting enough sleep, produces clear health advantages over time.

Doctors rely on both roots when explaining test results. If a lab scan finds a small growth that is benign, the patient breathes easier, because that word means harmless and unlikely to spread. By contrast, a malignant tumor is dangerous and likely to grow worse if left untreated. One small change in the root signals the difference between relief and urgent care.

The same roots describe machines and human character. When a traffic light suffers a malfunction, a sudden breakdown that stops the system from working properly, engineers look for a loose wire or faulty sensor—not a villain. People, however, can act with malice, a deliberate desire to cause hurt or embarrassment. Online, a malicious rumor spreads fast to damage someone's reputation, while a classic fairy-tale villain is often drawn as malevolent, wishing harm on everyone in the kingdom.

Fortunately, history is full of the opposite impulse. A benevolent neighbor acts with genuine kindness and generosity, looking for practical ways to help. When a retired librarian donates money to build a community reading room, she becomes a benefactor, and every child who borrows a book there is a beneficiary of her gift. From hospital charts to storybooks, bene and mal keep pointing readers toward what heals and what harms.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "benign" most nearly means
choices: spreading rapidly through nearby healthy tissue
harmless and unlikely to cause damage or spread
broken down because of a loose electrical wire
generous enough to fund a public reading room
qs.why: Paragraph 2 defines benign directly as "harmless and unlikely to spread."

qs.q: Which sentence shows the difference between a benefactor and a beneficiary?
choices: Fortunately, history is full of the opposite impulse.
A benevolent neighbor acts with genuine kindness and generosity, looking for practical ways to help.
When a retired librarian donates money to build a community reading room, she becomes a benefactor, and every child who borrows a book there is a beneficiary of her gift.
From hospital charts to storybooks, bene and mal keep pointing readers toward what heals and what harms.
qs.why: This sentence pairs the giver (the retired librarian, benefactor) with the receivers (every child who borrows a book, beneficiary).

ev.text: When a retired librarian donates money to build a community reading room, she becomes a benefactor, and every child who borrows a book there is a beneficiary of her gift.

qs.q: Why does the author note that engineers look for a loose wire, not a villain, during a malfunction?
choices: A malfunction is a mechanical failure rather than an act of human ill will.
Traffic lights rarely break down unless someone cuts their wires on purpose.
Engineers are not trained to recognize Latin roots when reading repair manuals.
Fairy-tale villains are more dangerous to towns than broken traffic signals.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 contrasts a mechanical malfunction with human malice, showing that mal can mean "badly working" as well as "evil."

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Doctors and engineers disagree about how Latin words should be spelled in modern charts.
Recognizing the Latin roots bene and mal helps readers understand many words about help and harm.
Donating money to build a library is the only true example of benevolent behavior in a town.
Fairy-tale villains are easier to understand than medical scans or broken traffic lights.
qs.why: The reading traces bene and mal across medicine, machines, character, and generosity to show how the roots unlock word meanings.
